brands.name: Raw Garden
brands.short: From the farm to the extract.
brands.text: Raw Garden traces its start to Santa Barbara County in 2015. Its own farm and extraction story is central to the brand: the company describes a seed-to-oil approach rather than sourcing a finished oil and placing a label on it.
brands.tip: Start with the extraction type. Refined live resin, live sauce and solventless live rosin are different product descriptions. Match the exact package to its published specifications before comparing price.
brands.question: Is this a cartridge, an all-in-one, or an extract that needs separate equipment?

brands.name: Kiva Confections
brands.text: Kiva is a California cannabis confectionery company with a portfolio spanning chocolates, gummies, mints and bites. Its product families include Kiva, Camino, Lost Farm, Petra and Terra. The name on the front of a package may therefore be a product family within a larger company.
brands.tip: Compare the individual piece and the whole package separately. Chocolate squares, mints and gummies are different formats, and a familiar brand name does not establish the amount in your particular package.
brands.question: What are the labeled milligrams per piece, and how many pieces are in this package?

brands.name: Camino
brands.short: Know the gummy behind the name.
brands.text: Camino is part of the Kiva portfolio. Its range includes gummies, sour gummies and fruit chews. The brand uses flavor, cannabinoid combinations and experience-oriented product names to distinguish its lines. Those names describe positioning, not a guaranteed personal response.
brands.tip: Read the exact variant. Products with similar artwork can carry different THC quantities or additional cannabinoids. Market-specific versions also differ, so use the California package and current local menu.
brands.question: Does this version contain CBD, CBN, CBG or another cannabinoid in addition to THC?

brands.name: WYLD
brands.short: Fruit-forward, with a label worth reading.
brands.text: WYLD presents itself as a nature-inspired edible brand built around fruit flavors. Its product range extends across multiple markets. For a San Jose shopper, the relevant comparison is the exact regulated California product rather than a package pictured on another state’s website.
brands.tip: Use ingredient lists to check dietary preferences. Compare cannabinoid ratios and package quantities before deciding that two flavors are equivalent. Flavor alone does not describe the full formulation.
brands.question: Am I comparing the same cannabinoid ratio and package size?

brands.name: PAX
brands.short: The device is part of the decision.
brands.text: PAX offers dry-herb vaporizers alongside oil-pod devices and cannabis products. Those are distinct systems. A device that uses loose flower is not the same as a battery designed for a prefilled oil pod.
brands.tip: Confirm hardware compatibility before buying. Look at the full device and pod names, whether a battery is included, and whether the item is a consumable product or reusable hardware.
brands.question: Will this product work with the device I already own?

brands.name: Jeeter
brands.text: Jeeter’s range includes pre-rolls and all-in-one vape products. Its own brand story emphasizes events, design and cannabis culture. When comparing its offerings, product construction is more informative than the size or color of a package.
brands.tip: Distinguish infused pre-rolls from flower-only products. Compare the number of units, total weight and ingredients. An all-in-one vape also has different replacement and disposal considerations from a rechargeable battery with a separate cartridge.
brands.question: What is added to the flower, and is the listed weight for one unit or the entire pack?

brands.name: Connected
brands.text: Connected traces its roots to Sacramento’s Fruitridge Health & Wellness Dispensary and describes launching the Connected brand in 2018. Its published history centers on cultivation and proprietary genetics, with a longstanding relationship with Alien Labs.
brands.tip: For flower, compare package date, batch information and weight alongside the cultivar name. A brand’s cultivation story gives context, but it cannot tell you the measured composition of every jar.
brands.question: Can I see the package date and the lab information for this exact batch?

brands.name: Alien Labs
brands.short: Genetics, culture, and the actual batch.
brands.text: Connected’s official history identifies Alien Labs as a longtime partner and a cultivation and lifestyle brand. The relationship is useful context for shoppers who see both names in a San Jose menu, but the brands should still be compared at the individual product level.
brands.tip: Do not treat cultivar names as fixed lab results. Check the product type, weight and batch documentation. Two packages with the same cultivar name can come from different harvests.
brands.question: Which characteristics are measured on the current batch, and which are general brand descriptions?

terpenes.name: Limonene
terpenes.text: Limonene is a useful starting point if you enjoy bright, peel-like aromas. This profile refers to the compound record identified below; limonene also has stereoisomers, which matter when interpreting chemical references.
terpenes.tip: A lemon-sounding cultivar name is not a limonene measurement. Ask for the terpene panel for the actual batch.

terpenes.name: Myrcene
terpenes.text: Myrcene is frequently discussed when people describe earthy, herbal cannabis aromas. Its presence is a chemical observation, not a reliable instruction about how a product will feel.
terpenes.tip: Compare its reported concentration with the rest of the panel. The largest individual terpene is only one part of a mixture.

terpenes.name: Alpha-pinene
terpenes.text: Alpha-pinene belongs to the pine-like end of the aroma vocabulary. Alpha-pinene and beta-pinene are distinct compounds, so a lab report may list them separately.
terpenes.tip: Keep alpha-pinene and beta-pinene separate when copying lab results. A combined pinene figure should say clearly that it combines both.

terpenes.name: Linalool
terpenes.text: Linalool is associated with floral fragrance descriptions. This guide uses floral as a sensory reference, not a claim that a cannabis product treats anxiety, sleep problems or any other condition.
terpenes.tip: Read the measured amount and the report units. A familiar floral association does not establish the dominant aroma of a whole product.

terpenes.name: Beta-caryophyllene
terpenes.text: Beta-caryophyllene sits in the spicy, woody part of this explorer. PubChem identifies it as a sesquiterpene, a different molecular class from monoterpenes such as myrcene.
terpenes.tip: Check whether the panel lists beta-caryophyllene or caryophyllene oxide. They are separate compounds and should not be merged without explanation.

terpenes.name: Humulene
terpenes.text: Humulene, also called alpha-caryophyllene, is a sesquiterpene. Its naming makes it easy to confuse with beta-caryophyllene, which has a different compound record.
terpenes.tip: Look for alternate names on reports. Avoid double-counting humulene and alpha-caryophyllene if a source uses both for the same compound.

terpenes.name: Terpinolene
terpenes.text: Terpinolene spans several aroma descriptors rather than fitting neatly into one box. The aroma chips in this explorer are editorial categories that help compare descriptions, not measured intensity scores.
terpenes.tip: A product can contain several terpenes with overlapping descriptors. Choose a profile to investigate, then check the current lab panel.

terpenes.name: Beta-pinene
terpenes.text: Beta-pinene is a distinct isomer of pinene. Sharing a molecular formula with another compound does not make the compounds identical or their sensory contributions interchangeable.
terpenes.tip: If a report says only pinene, ask whether it identifies an isomer or combines values. Record the laboratory’s wording exactly.

guides: edible-families
The edible field guide: look past the flavor.
The edible edit
A practical way to compare gummies, chocolate, mints and chews without relying on the package name.
Start with the unit you are comparing

An edible has at least three useful identities: its food format, its cannabinoid formulation and its package configuration. A gummy and a mint can have the same labeled THC amount while differing in ingredients, size and the number of pieces in the package. First write down the milligrams per piece, the number of pieces and the whole-package amount. A front-of-package number without its unit is not enough for a meaningful comparison.
Read a fictional shelf side by side

Imagine package A contains ten pieces labeled 5 mg THC each, and package B contains five pieces labeled 10 mg each. Both contain 50 mg in total, but they are not the same piece-level product. This arithmetic is an example for reading labels, not a suggested amount to consume. Next check whether additional cannabinoids are listed. A product with THC and CBD should not be summarized by its THC number alone.
Make room for the ingredient list

Texture and flavor are not the only food details. Look at the actual ingredient and allergen statements when checking a dietary preference. Do not infer that all products within one brand family share a recipe. Chocolate, gelatin-based gummies and pectin-based gummies are different food constructions, and a brand can offer more than one. The current package is more relevant than a photo from a different state or an old product announcement.
Use the brand family as a map

Kiva’s portfolio includes several distinct families, including Camino, Petra, Terra and Lost Farm. That relationship helps you navigate a menu; it does not make their packages interchangeable. Compare a specific California product with another specific California product. BAYLEAF’s shortlist groups documented formats so you can decide which profiles to read next. It is not an inventory feed or a recommendation of a personal serving.
Leave with a better question

A useful question is: “Can you show me the piece amount, total package amount and other cannabinoids on this exact version?” That invites a concrete answer. Save the brand names you want to investigate, then return to the current retailer menu for the exact items. Source basis: Kiva’s official portfolio and the California Department of Cannabis Control consumer and labeling resources linked on our Sources page.
device-compatibility
The five-minute hardware check.
Devices & formats
Sort out dry herb, pods, cartridges and all-in-one products before comparing a price.
Name the system before the brand

Start with what the hardware takes as its input. A dry-herb device takes loose flower. An oil-pod device takes its compatible pod. A cartridge system takes an appropriate cartridge and battery. An all-in-one combines oil and hardware in one product. A familiar manufacturer name does not mean these systems share consumables. PAX, for example, has both dry-herb products and an ERA pod ecosystem.
Write down the complete model

“I have a PAX” is less useful than the full device model. Record the exact device and the exact product you are researching, including generation or model qualifiers. Use the manufacturer’s compatibility information to check the pair. A menu thumbnail may show a battery for illustration even when the item for sale is only a pod. Read the item description for what is included in the box.
Compare like with like

A standalone consumable and a kit with reusable hardware have different upfront costs. If you already own compatible hardware, that changes the comparison. If you do not, include the required device in your research budget. Do not treat the lowest menu price as a complete setup without checking this. Capacity also needs a unit: the oil amount is separate from battery capacity and neither is a measure of how a product will feel.
Plan for the end of the product

Reusable hardware, an empty cartridge and a depleted all-in-one are different objects. Follow the manufacturer’s and local waste authority’s current handling guidance for batteries and cannabis vaping products. Do not assume that a small electronic device belongs in household recycling. California’s cannabis labeling resources include specific guidance on vape disposal language.
A checklist you can use at the counter

Bring the model name and ask: Is this the correct consumable? Is the battery included? What charging equipment does it require? Where are the official care and end-of-life instructions? This turns a broad brand preference into a compatibility check that can be answered. See the PAX profile and our official Sources page for the starting points.
brand-family-tree
Different names. Connected stories.
Brand culture
How to use brand relationships without confusing a parent company, a product family and a batch.
A name can sit at several levels

Cannabis menus mix company names, product families and individual product names in the same visual space. A family of gummy products may have a strong identity of its own while belonging to a larger confectionery business. Knowing that structure makes research easier: you can find a manufacturer’s full portfolio and then locate the exact family. It does not make all products in the portfolio identical.
The Kiva and Camino example

Kiva’s official portfolio includes Camino alongside Kiva chocolates, Petra, Terra and Lost Farm. BAYLEAF includes both Kiva and Camino because a consumer may encounter either name on a San Jose menu. When both appear in a shortlist, read them as different levels of the same documented family. We do not count their shared relationship as evidence of two independent manufacturers competing with each other.
The Connected and Alien Labs example

Connected’s published history discusses its Northern California cultivation roots and relationship with Alien Labs. That shared story is useful cultural context. A Connected package and an Alien Labs package still need their own product-level comparison: format, weight, packaging date and batch information. A corporate or cultivation relationship does not prove that two jars have the same contents or measured composition.
Keep the source date in view

Relationships, portfolios and product availability can change. Our source checks revisit the official pages monthly and display their status. A successful page check means the source was reachable; it is not a legal audit of ownership or a guarantee that every product line remains available. We identify relationships only to the level supported by the cited official account. When a source is unclear, uncertainty is more useful than an elaborate family tree built on guesswork.
Turn a relationship into a question

Ask whether the name you see identifies the manufacturer, a product family or a specific variant. Then ask which source describes the exact item you are buying. The answer helps you move from a brand story to verifiable package details. Our brand profiles link directly to the official histories so you can inspect the original wording yourself.
glossary: Batch
A particular production lot. Its documentation is more specific than a general brand story.
Product family
A named group within a company’s portfolio, such as Camino within Kiva.
Format
The physical product type, such as flower, edible, pod or pre-roll.
All-in-one
A product combining its oil and vaping hardware. Check charging and disposal instructions.
Pod
A consumable designed for a compatible pod device. Check the complete model name.
Infused pre-roll
A pre-roll with added cannabis material such as an extract; read the ingredient description.
COA
Certificate of analysis. Match it to the product or batch before using its measurements.
Cultivar
A named cultivated variety. Its name does not provide a fixed laboratory composition.
Package amount
The amount across the full package, which can differ from the amount in one piece.
Shortlist
A saved set of profiles to investigate, not a quality ranking or stock reservation.
